l: 3. Changing a setting while the program runs
p: A command like !prefix ? should write the change back to disk so it survives a restart.
set_path creates the section if the server has never been configured, so there is no "does this server exist yet" branch to write.

save() writes to a temporary file next to the real one and renames it into place. A crash mid-write leaves the old config intact rather than a truncated one, and a reader never catches the file half-written. You get that without asking for it.
Comments are lost. The moment a program saves a file, every # note in it is gone. Keep hand-annotated files separate from the ones your program owns — recipe 6 shows the usual split.
Saving is not a queue. If several parts of your program save the same config at once, the last write wins. For anything concurrent, funnel saves through one place.

p: Four things, all of them JavaScript's doing rather than JPCL's:
Python has unlimited integers; Go has int64. This is the one you are most likely to trip over.
There is one number type, so 1.0 reads back as 1 and is written as 1.
Integer-like keys move to the front

JavaScript objects always enumerate keys such as 1234567890 first, in ascending order, before every other key. A [1234567890] section therefore comes out ahead of [SERVER_ID] even if the file had it last. Pass a Map to dumps if that order matters.
Object properties holding undefined are skipped, and undefined array elements become null — the same rules as JSON.stringify.
The first three are also listed under Round trips.
JPConfig methods: get, set, has, delete, keys, values, entries, size, data, getPath, setPath, hasPath, section, merge, toObject, dumps, save, saveSync, reload, reloadSync.

p: Complete projects using all of this.
No runtime dependencies — standard library only. Go 1.27+.

The format and the error messages are identical to the Python and TypeScript implementations. The API leans on Go idioms rather than mirroring their syntax, and this page is mostly about where those idioms show through.

c: go get github.com/jpcl-lang/jpcl-go

p: Values are carried around as any, so reading a nested value means a type assertion at each step. That is Go, not JPCL — see Getting at values for the tidy way to do it.

Go's built-in map does not preserve insertion order, and the writer needs to reproduce keys in the order they were written. jpcl.Object is a small ordered-map type the package defines for that reason:

There is no obj[key] syntax, because Go has no operator overloading. There is also no map[string]any support in the writer — building a document means calling Set, not writing a map literal, so the ordering guarantee always holds.

c:
obj := jpcl.NewObject()
obj.Set("prefix", "!")
obj.Set("id", int64(1234567890))

value, ok := obj.Get("prefix")   // "!", true
obj.Len()                        // 2
for _, key := range obj.Keys() { // "prefix", then "id" -- insertion order
	fmt.Println(key)
}

p: Integers are int64, not arbitrary precision like Python's int and not bigint-backed like JavaScript's. A number larger than roughly 9.2×10^18 loses precision by falling through to float64.
That is fine for Discord snowflakes, which top out well below it, but it is a real limit to know about if you need bigger integers. Integer width compares all three.

c:
data, err := jpcl.Load("data/servers.jp", jpcl.ParseOptions{})   // from a path
data, err := jpcl.Parse(text, jpcl.ParseOptions{})               // from a string

p: DuplicateError is the zero value, so a bare jpcl.ParseOptions{} gives you the strict default — a repeated key is an error rather than a silent overwrite. See Duplicate keys.
Reaching into a parsed document by hand is verbose:
Each of those assertions panics if the shape isn't what you assumed. For anything beyond one level, use JPConfig.GetPath instead — it walks the path safely and returns your default at any depth:
One assertion instead of four, and no panic on a missing section.

c:
section, _ := data.Get("SERVER_ID")
config, _ := section.(*jpcl.Object).Get("config")
users, _ := config.(*jpcl.Object).Get("disabled_users")
list := users.([]any)

cfg, _ := jpcl.LoadJPConfig("data/servers.jp", false, jpcl.ConfigOptions{})
users := cfg.GetPath("SERVER_ID.config.disabled_users", []any{}).([]any)

p: The arguments are directory, glob pattern ( means *.jp), recursive, and parse options.

Each file becomes one entry, named after the file without its .jp suffix. The returned value is a plain Go map, since it is a lookup table rather than a document you write back out — unlike *jpcl.Object, its iteration order is not meaningful.

c:
text, err := jpcl.Dumps(obj, jpcl.DefaultStringifyOptions())
err = jpcl.Dump(obj, "data/servers.jp", true, jpcl.DefaultStringifyOptions()) // atomic

p: Go structs have no default field values, so a bare StringifyOptions{} means Indent: 0, Width: 0 — indistinguishable from an explicit choice, and it produces unindented output with every array broken across lines.
This is the single most common mistake with the Go package.
c: opts := jpcl.DefaultStringifyOptions() // {Indent: 2, Width: 88} opts.SortKeys = true text, err := jpcl.Dumps(obj, opts)

type StringifyOptions struct {
	Indent      int                 // spaces per level
	Width       int                 // column budget for inline arrays
	SortKeys    bool                // sort keys alphabetically instead of insertion order
	EnsureASCII bool                // escape non-ASCII characters
	Default     func(value any) any // convert otherwise-unsupported types
}

p: For types .jp has no representation for — time.Time, a custom struct, anything else:
It must return a different type from the one it was handed, or you get default() returned an unconverted ....

Dump's third argument is atomic. With true, the file goes to a temporary neighbour and is renamed into place, so a crash or a concurrent reader never sees half a config. Missing parent directories are created.

l: Editing a config in place: JPConfig
p: JPConfig wraps an *Object and remembers the file it came from, adding dotted-path access and atomic saving. Its backing store is a public field, Data, since Go has no subscript operator to stand in for Python's cfg[key]:

c:
cfg, err := jpcl.LoadJPConfig("data/servers.jp", true, jpcl.ConfigOptions{
	Write: jpcl.DefaultStringifyOptions(),
})
// missingOK: true -- an empty config bound to the path if it doesn't exist yet

prefix, _ := cfg.Data.Get("SERVER_ID")                            // plain Object access
cfg.GetPath("SERVER_ID.config.disabled_users", []any{})           // never fails on a missing section
cfg.SetPath("SERVER_ID.config.disabled_users", []any{int64(9892)}) // creates missing sections
cfg.HasPath("SERVER_ID.prefix")
sec, _ := cfg.Section("NEW_SERVER", true)                          // create: true
sec.Set("prefix", "?")
cfg.Merge(other, true)  // deep merge
cfg.Save("")            // atomic, back to its own bound path
cfg.Reload()            // discard in-memory changes
cfg.ToDict()            // deep copy as a plain *Object

p: missingOK: true gives an empty config bound to the path, which is what a program that writes its config on first run wants:

c:
jpcl.LoadJPConfig(path, missingOK, opts)   // read a file
jpcl.LoadsJPConfig(text, path, opts)       // from a string, optionally bound to a path
jpcl.NewJPConfig(obj, opts)                // from data you already have

p: SetPath returns an error only when a path segment holds something that isn't a section — cannot descend into a.b: it holds string, not a section. Section returns an error if the name is missing without create, or holds a non-section.

c:
cfg.GetPath("SERVER_ID.config.disabled_users", []any{})  // returns the default at any depth
err := cfg.SetPath("SERVER_ID.prefix", "!")              // creates missing levels
cfg.HasPath("SERVER_ID.prefix")
sec, err := cfg.Section("SERVER_ID", false)              // error if missing
sec, err := cfg.Section("NEW_SERVER", true)              // created empty if missing

p: Save() on a config with no bound path is an error.

Unlike the Python and TypeScript versions, formatting options live in ConfigOptions.Write and are fixed when the config is built — Save and Dumps always use them, with no per-call override. Again, this avoids the zero-value ambiguity. For a one-off different format, call the package-level function directly:
c: text, err := jpcl.Dumps(cfg.Data, customOpts)

path, err := cfg.Save("")             // back to the bound path
path, err := cfg.Save("backup.jp")    // somewhere else; the config rebinds to it
text, err := cfg.Dumps()              // just the text
cfg.FilePath()                        // (path, bound bool)
cfg.SetFilePath("data/other.jp")

It carries Message, Doc, Pos, Line, Col and Filename, and implements error:

When it goes wrong lists every message and what to do about each.

Flags must come before positional arguments — jpcl fmt -w file.jp, not jpcl fmt file.jp -w. Go's standard flag package stops looking for flags at the first non-flag argument.
This is the one place the Go CLI is a step behind the Python (argparse) and TypeScript (util.parseArgs) versions, which accept either order.

Print only failures. Successes are silent.
A failure goes to stderr with the exact position:
Checking stops at the first error in each file, but carries on to the next file, so one run tells you which files are broken even if it doesn't list every fault within them.
jpcl check data/*.jp is a one-line CI step that catches a broken config before it reaches production. It exits 1 on any failure, which is all most CI systems need.

p: Column budget before an inline array breaks onto several lines.
Reformat files to canonical style. Without -w, the result goes to stdout and the file is untouched.
Reformatting is a parse followed by a write, and the writer does not reproduce comments. Running jpcl fmt -w over a hand-annotated file will silently delete every # note in it.
Rewrite each file in place instead of printing.
Run jpcl fmt without -w first and read the output if you are not sure what a file will lose.
Sort keys alphabetically instead of keeping the order they were written in.

With -w, a file that is already correctly formatted is left completely alone — not rewritten with identical content — so timestamps and file watchers stay quiet. Files that did change are reported on stderr:

jpcl fmt -w data/servers.jp       # rewrite it in place
jpcl fmt -w --indent 4 data/*.jp
reformatted data/servers.jp

p: Print one value, addressed by a dotted path.
Print strings unquoted. Has no effect on other types.
The value is printed as JSON, which means strings come out quoted:
-r is what you want in a shell script:

Useful for feeding a .jp config to anything that only speaks JSON, and for seeing exactly what your file parses to when the answer is surprising.

Every top-level object in the JSON becomes a [SECTION]. Top-level scalars are hoisted above the first section — see Round trips.
from-json is the quickest way to move an existing JSON config over:
Then open the result and add the comments JSON never let you write.
Write to a file instead of printing.

p: A file failed to parse, a path didn't exist, or a file couldn't be read or written.
The command line itself was wrong — unknown subcommand, missing argument, unrecognised flag.
Print usage. Works on the top level and on each subcommand: jpcl fmt --help.
Every message JPCL can produce, what it actually means, and how to fix it. The messages are the same in all three implementations, so this page applies whichever one you are using.

One cosmetic difference: Go quotes names with double quotes (expected ':' after key prefix) where Python and JavaScript use single quotes ('prefix'). The messages are otherwise word-for-word identical, and this page uses the Python spelling.
JPCL points at the exact character that upset it:
The file. stdin if it came from a pipe.

The caret is the whole diagnosis. Look at the character it points at, then at the character before it, and the answer is almost always there. The line number is where JPCL noticed, which for an unclosed bracket is later than where you actually went wrong — but the message for those says where the bracket opened.
If you want to render the failure yourself, the error object carries .line, .col, .pos, .filename and the raw message. See your language's page for the field names.

c:
data/servers.jp:2:8: expected ':' after key 'prefix', found '"'
    prefix "!"
           ^

p: Raised when a file cannot be read. JPDecodeError in Python and JavaScript, *jpcl.DecodeError in Go.
There is a key, but no colon after it.

c:
# WRONG
prefix "!"

# WRONG -- JPCL uses ':', not '='
prefix = "!"

# RIGHT
prefix: "!"

p: Something appeared where a key was expected — usually a stray bracket or an opening brace with no key in front of it.
If the message says found end of file, the document ended mid-entry — usually an unclosed { much further up that swallowed the rest of the file.

l: expected ',', a line break or ']' after value, found ...
p: A value was read, then something that can't follow it. The '}' and "or a line break" variants are the same problem inside an object, or at the top level of a section.

Between two unquoted values, the missing comma is absorbed instead. {rate: 30 burst: 5} is valid, and gives you one key whose value is the string 30 burst: 5 — because an unquoted value runs until a comma, a bracket, a # or a line break. If a value comes back as unexpected text, look for a missing comma before you look anywhere else.

c:
# WRONG -- no comma between the two
roles: ["moderator" "admin"]

# RIGHT
roles: ["moderator", "admin"]

p: A { was opened and never closed. The position points at where the object started, not at the end of the file.

c:
# WRONG
roles: [111, 222

p: Your brackets are crossed — an array was closed with a brace. The position points at where the array opened.
It usually means a bracket further up is the wrong kind, not that this one is. Count your { and [ from the top of the section.

c:
# WRONG
roles: [111, 222,}

p: A [ opened a header and no ] closed it before the line ended.

c:
# WRONG
[SERVER_ID

l: section header cannot be empty / section header segment cannot be empty
p: [], or a dotted header with a gap in it.

c:
# WRONG
[]
[guild.]
[.limits]
[guild..limits]

# RIGHT
[guild.limits]

p: Something other than a line break followed the ].

c:
# WRONG
[SERVER_ID] prefix: "!"

# RIGHT
[SERVER_ID]
prefix: "!"

l: expected a line break before a section header
p: A [HEADER] appeared on the same line as the entry before it. A header always starts its own line.

c:
# WRONG
[SERVER_ID]
prefix: "!" [SERVER_ID_2]

p: The same key appears twice in the same object.
Decide which one you meant and delete the other. If you genuinely want the later value to win, load the file with the duplicate policy set to last — see Duplicate keys.

c:
# WRONG
[SERVER_ID]
prefix: "!"
prefix: "?"

p: The same section header appears twice. Merge the two by hand, or load with the last policy, which merges them for you.
A header tried to nest inside something that isn't an object.

c:
# WRONG -- guild is a number, so [guild.limits] has nowhere to go
guild: 1

[guild.limits]
rate: 30

p: A quote was opened and the file ended before it closed.

Watch for a stray inside a string — the second quote closes it early and the third opens a new one that never ends. If the string had a line break in it rather than running to the end of the file, you get the longer message below instead.

c:
# WRONG -- and the file stops right there
name: "Clanker

l: unterminated string literal (use \n for a line break)
p: A quoted string ran into an actual line break.

c:
# WRONG
message: "first line
second line"

# RIGHT
message: "first line\nsecond line"

# ALSO RIGHT -- a trailing backslash continues the literal
message: "first line \
second line"

p: A \ followed by something JPCL doesn't recognise.
To mean a literal backslash, double it: a\\qb. Escape sequences lists everything that is valid after a backslash.

c:
# WRONG
k: "a\qb"

l: '\u...' escape needs 4 hex digits / '\U...' escape needs 8 hex digits
p: A Unicode escape was cut short. \u takes exactly four hex digits, \U exactly eight — pad with leading zeros: \U0001F600.
The usual cause is not a Unicode escape at all, but a Windows path:

c:
# WRONG -- \U is read as the start of an 8-digit escape
path: "C:\Users\notes"

# RIGHT -- double the backslashes
path: "C:\\Users\\notes"

# ALSO RIGHT -- forward slashes work on Windows too
path: "C:/Users/notes"

l: '\u...' is an unpaired surrogate / '\U...' is outside the Unicode range
p: The escape names something that isn't a valid character. Half of a surrogate pair, or a code point above U+10FFFF. Write the character itself instead, or use the correct code point.
The file ended immediately after a \.

{ and [ may nest 200 deep. If you have hit this legitimately, the structure wants flattening — dotted section headers are usually the answer. If you have hit it accidentally, you probably have a missing } somewhere and JPCL has been descending ever since.

Raised when your program hands JPCL something it cannot put in a file. JPEncodeError in Python and JavaScript, *jpcl.EncodeError in Go. These are bugs in the calling code rather than problems with a file.

l: object of type '...' is not serialisable to .jp; pass default= to convert it
p: You tried to write a value JPCL has no representation for — a datetime, a set, a class instance, a function.
Supply a default hook that converts it:
c: jpcl.dumps(data, default=str) # or something more deliberate def convert(value): if isinstance(value, datetime): return value.isoformat() raise TypeError(value) jpcl.dumps(data, default=convert)
jpcl.dumps(data, { default: (v) => (v instanceof Date ? v.toISOString() : String(v)), });
opts := jpcl.DefaultStringifyOptions() opts.Default = func(v any) any { if t, ok := v.(time.Time); ok { return t.Format(time.RFC3339) } return fmt.Sprint(v) } text, err := jpcl.Dumps(obj, opts)

p: Your default hook handed back the same type it was given, which would loop forever. Return something JPCL can write — a string is nearly always the right answer.

l: binary data has no .jp representation; decode or encode it to a string first
p: You passed bytes (Python), a Buffer/Uint8Array (JavaScript) or []byte (Go). .jp is a text format. Decode it if it's text, or base64-encode it if it isn't.

l: keys must be strings (or ints), got '...'
p: An object key was something else — a tuple, an object, None. Integer keys are fine and become strings on the way out, which is why [1234567890] sections round-trip.
Something in the structure contains itself, directly or through a chain. A shared reference that isn't a cycle is fine — the same list appearing under two keys writes out twice, without complaint.

l: the top level of a .jp document must be a mapping, got '...'
p: You passed a list, a string or a number to dumps. The top level of a .jp document is always an object, because top-level values become [SECTION] headers. Wrap it: {items: [...]}.
load_dir was pointed at a path that doesn't exist or isn't a directory. Check the path is relative to where the program runs, not to where the source file lives — this catches everyone at least once.

l: this config has no path to reload from / this config has no path; call save(path) or set .path first
p: You called reload() or save() on a JPConfig that was built from a string rather than loaded from a file, so it has no path to work with. Pass a path to save(), set .path, or construct the config with one.
A negative indent was passed to the writer.
A typo'd option name. The message lists what it didn't recognise — check the spelling and the case convention for your language (sort_keys in Python, sortKeys in JavaScript).

l: Problems that produce no error at all
p: The hard ones. Nothing crashes; the file is just not what you meant.

l: My value came out as a string
p: An unquoted value is read as a keyword, then as a number, then as text. If it isn't one of the first two, it's text.
true, false, null, none, nil, inf, infinity and nan are the keywords. yes, no, on and off are not.

c:
version: 1.2.3      # string "1.2.3" -- not a number, so it stays text
enabled: yes        # string "yes" -- 'yes' is not a keyword; use true
count: 1_000        # integer 1000 -- underscores are separators
id: "42"            # string "42" -- the quotes win

l: My value came out as null
p: You wrote the value on the line after the colon:
The opening bracket must sit on the colon's line. See Empty values for why.
An unquoted value stops at a #, a comma, or a closing bracket. With a #, the rest is read as a comment and silently discarded:
With a comma it usually errors instead, because what follows is read as the next key:

c:
label: issue #1 reported
# -> label is "issue"

csv: a, b, c
# -> expected ':' after key 'b', found ','

label: "issue #1 reported"
csv: "a, b, c"

p: Something rewrote the file. jpcl fmt -w, or a program calling save() or dump(). The writer reproduces data, not annotations.
Keep hand-annotated files separate from the files your program writes to. A common split is a committed servers.example.jp full of comments, and a live servers.jp that the program owns.

l: My sections came back in a different order
p: In JavaScript, keys that look like integers are always enumerated first, in ascending order, before everything else. That is the language, not JPCL. A [1234567890] section will come out ahead of [SERVER_ID] however you wrote it. Pass a Map to dumps if that order matters.
In any implementation, sort_keys was switched on somewhere.

l: A root-level key moved to the top of the file
p: That is deliberate. A scalar written after a header would read back as part of that section, so the writer hoists all root-level scalars above the first header. The data is unchanged. See Round trips.
JavaScript only. It has a single number type, so a whole float is indistinguishable from an integer. Python and Go keep the distinction.

l: A big ID lost its last few digits
p: You are in Go, where integers are int64, and the value exceeded it — or in JavaScript with integers: number forced on. In JavaScript's default mode, anything past 2^53 arrives as a bigint and stays exact. See Integer width.

l: My edits to the file do nothing
p: Most programs read their config once, at startup. Restart it. If it still ignores you, check you are editing the file the program actually loads — print the resolved path at startup and you will usually find the answer immediately.
Three things worth trying, in order:

The precise version of the format: what the parser accepts, what it produces, and what the writer guarantees. This is the page to read if you are implementing JPCL yourself, or if you need to know exactly where a boundary lies.
For the same rules explained conversationally, read Writing .jp files.
A .jp document is an ordered mapping of string keys to values.
Key order is insertion order, and is preserved through a round trip. Go's built-in map does not preserve order, which is why the Go implementation defines its own ordered Object type.
Documents are UTF-8. A leading UTF-8 byte-order mark is stripped if present. Both \n and \r\n line endings are accepted.
Spaces and tabs separate tokens and are otherwise insignificant. Line breaks are significant: they terminate an entry and terminate a bare token.
A comment may appear anywhere a token may appear, including inside {} and []. It runs to the end of the line and is discarded.

The captured run is then trimmed of surrounding whitespace. A bare key may therefore contain spaces and dots; a bare value may contain spaces, dots, colons and brackets' worth of other punctuation, but not a comma, a closing brace or bracket, or a #.
Either or ' opens a string; the same character closes it. The two are interchangeable and carry no difference in meaning or escaping.
An unescaped line break inside a string is an error (unterminated string literal (use \n for a line break)). Use \n, or a trailing \ to continue the literal onto the next source line.
Anything else after a \ is invalid escape sequence. A \uXXXX that names an unpaired surrogate, or a \UXXXXXXXX outside the Unicode range, is rejected rather than replaced.

Separators are greedy: any run of commas and line breaks counts as one separator, so leading, repeated and trailing commas are all accepted and carry no meaning.

c:
document    = *( entry-sep ) [ root-entries ] *( section )
root-entries= entry *( entry-sep entry )
section     = header *( entry-sep ) [ entries ]
header      = "[" segment *( "." segment ) "]"
segment     = bare-segment / quoted
entry       = key ":" [ value ]
key         = bare-key / quoted
value       = object / array / quoted / bare-value
object      = "{" [ members ] "}"
members     = entry *( entry-sep entry ) [ entry-sep ]
array       = "[" [ elements ] "]"
elements    = value *( element-sep value ) [ element-sep ]
entry-sep   = 1*( "," / line-break )
element-sep = 1*( "," / line-break )

p: A value must begin on the same line as its :. Once begun, an object or array may span as many lines as it likes.

This follows directly from empty values being legal. timeout: followed by a line break is a complete entry with the value null; there is no lookahead that could distinguish it from a value that was going to appear on the next line.
An unquoted value is resolved in this order:
Empty — an empty or whitespace-only token yields null.
Keyword — matched case-insensitively against the table below.
Case-insensitivity is deliberate: True, None and NULL all work, so a file written by someone thinking in Python or in JSON parses either way.
Underscores are permitted as digit separators in any of these. A token that starts like a number but does not parse as one falls through to being a string — 1.2.3 is the string 1.2.3, not an error.
The format itself places no limit on integer size; the implementations do, differently:
An integer that fits in a number exactly (up to 253) becomes one; beyond that it becomes a bigint, so no digit is ever silently changed. Configurable with the integers option.
int64. A value beyond roughly 9.2×1018 falls through to float64 and loses precision.
Discord snowflakes and other 64-bit IDs are the usual reason this matters. They are safe in all three, but in JavaScript they arrive as bigint.
A header's segments are resolved left to right, creating objects as needed.
A segment that already names an object descends into it.
A segment that already names a non-object is an error: cannot open section '[...]': ....
Re-opening a section that already exists is section '[...]' is defined twice, unless the duplicate-key policy is last, in which case the two are merged.
A header segment may not be empty: [], [a.] and [.a] are all errors.
Entries appearing before the first header attach to the document root. There is no syntax for returning to the root after a header has opened.
Within one object, a repeated key is governed by the parse-time policy:
first section kept, later entries ignored

{ and [ may nest to 200 levels. Beyond that the parser refuses with nesting deeper than 200 levels. The cap exists so that a hostile or accidentally generated document cannot exhaust the stack; no legitimate config comes close.
In the JavaScript implementation, a key named __proto__ is defined as an ordinary own property rather than being allowed to replace an object's prototype. A .jp file cannot cause prototype pollution.
The writer is deterministic: the same input always produces byte-identical output, so a file written twice does not churn in version control.
Every top-level object value becomes a [SECTION], separated by a blank line.
Section entries sit one per line, with no separating commas.
Nested objects always expand across lines. {} is the only inline object form.
Arrays stay inline while they fit within width (default 88 columns), then break one element per line.
Null is written as an empty value inside objects (key:) and as null inside arrays, since an array element cannot be empty.
Keys are quoted only when they must be.
Insertion order is preserved unless sortKeys / sort_keys / SortKeys is set.

File-writing functions write to a temporary neighbour and rename it into place. A crash or a concurrent reader therefore never sees a half-written config. Missing parent directories are created.
Parse → write → parse is lossless for data. Two things do not survive a rewrite in any implementation:
The writer reproduces values, not annotations. A hand-annotated file loses its notes when a program saves it.
Root scalars move to the top
They are hoisted above the first section, because anything after a header would read back as part of that section. The data is unchanged; its position in the file is not.
JavaScript adds two of its own, both inherited from the language:
Integer-like keys move to the front
JavaScript objects always enumerate keys such as 1234567890 first, in ascending order, before every other key. Pass a Map to dumps if the order of such keys matters.
There is one number type, so 1.0 reads back as 1 and is written as 1.
Everything else — key order, types, structure, string content — comes back identical, and a file written by any implementation is read identically by the other two.
